title: Topological Sort — Kahn's & DFS-Based
summary: Topological sort orders every node so dependencies come first, using two genuinely different mechanisms — peeling zero-in-degree nodes layer by layer, or reversing a DFS post-order — that also double as free cycle detectors.

slides.markdown:
A **topological order** arranges every node in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) so that every edge `u → v` has `u` appearing before `v` — every dependency comes before whatever depends on it. Build systems, course prerequisites, and task schedulers are all topological-sort problems wearing different clothes.

Two algorithms produce a valid order via genuinely different mechanisms: **Kahn's algorithm** peels off zero-in-degree nodes layer by layer using a queue, and **DFS-based sort** takes a post-order traversal and reverses it. Both cost O(V+E), both only work on a DAG, and — this is the connection worth knowing cold — both double as a cycle detector for free, since a cycle makes a full topological order impossible.

A topological order guarantees exactly one thing: for every directed edge `u → v`, `u` appears somewhere before `v` in the output. It does **not** guarantee that `u` immediately precedes `v`, and it does **not** guarantee a unique answer — most DAGs have many valid topological orders, and any of them is equally correct.

This matters because candidates sometimes over-promise what the order encodes — a topological order tells you a valid sequence to process dependencies in, not the *only* valid sequence, and not anything about which nodes could run in parallel (that's a separate question, related to but not answered directly by the order alone).

slides.sectionTitle: Kahn's algorithm: peel off zero-in-degree layers
slides.markdown:
Compute every node's **in-degree** (number of incoming edges). Any node with in-degree 0 has no unfulfilled dependencies, so it's safe to place next in the order. Put all such nodes in a queue, then repeatedly: dequeue a node, add it to the output, and decrement the in-degree of each of its neighbors — any neighbor that drops to in-degree 0 as a result gets added to the queue.

This naturally processes the graph in **layers**: everything with in-degree 0 initially, then everything that becomes in-degree 0 once the first layer is removed, and so on — directly mirroring a real dependency-resolution process ("what can I build right now, given what's already done").

Run a standard DFS, and every time a node **finishes** (all its descendants have been fully explored), push it onto a stack. Once DFS has visited every node, pop the stack — that pop order is a valid topological order.

The intuition: a node only finishes after everything reachable from it has already finished, meaning everything it points to is already "done" and sitting lower in the finish-order stack — so reversing that order puts dependencies before dependents, exactly the topological property required.

slides.sectionTitle: In-degree layers vs finishing times reversed
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: a small DAG with 6 nodes shown twice; left side labelled Kahn's shows nodes grouped into three horizontal layers by when their in-degree hits 0, with an arrow showing the queue draining layer by layer; right side labelled DFS-based shows the same DAG with a finish-time number next to each node from a DFS run, and an arrow showing those numbers reversed to produce the final order >>>

Both arrive at a valid order — often a *different* valid order from each other, since a DAG can have many correct topological orderings and neither algorithm is obligated to find the same one.

For any edge `u → v` in a DAG, DFS from `u` (or a call reaching `u` before `v`) must finish `v` before it finishes `u` — because `v` is reachable from `u`, DFS has to fully explore `v` (and everything below it) as part of exploring `u`'s subtree, before `u` itself can be marked finished.

So in the raw finish order, `v` always finishes before `u` for every edge `u → v`. Reversing that order puts `u` before `v` for every such edge — exactly the topological property. This is a real proof sketch, not just an observed pattern, and it's worth being able to state out loud if asked "why does this work" rather than just "what do you do."

| | Kahn's algorithm | DFS-based |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | In-degree + queue, layer by layer | Post-order + reverse |
| Cycle detection | Free — output length < n means a cycle | Needs an added gray/black check (three-color method) |
| Natural extra output | Layers = groups that could run in parallel | None extra, just the order |
| Style | Iterative, BFS-flavored | Recursive (or manually iterative), DFS-flavored |

Kahn's edge: cycle detection falls out of the algorithm's own bookkeeping (the length check), and the layering it naturally produces is a genuine bonus — it directly answers "what can happen in parallel at each stage," which the DFS version doesn't expose without extra work.

Topological sort isn't an academic exercise — it's the literal algorithm behind: **build systems** (compile module B only after its dependency module A), **course scheduling** (take a prerequisite course before the one that requires it), **task schedulers** (run job Y only after job X completes), and package managers resolving install order from a dependency graph.

Every one of these systems either runs a topological sort directly or is quietly relying on the same guarantee under a different name — "dependency resolution," "build order," "install order" are all topological sort by another name.

slides.sectionTitle: Uniqueness, and skipping the cycle check
slides.markdown:
Two mistakes worth naming together. First: assuming a topological order is **unique** — it almost never is, and code that depends on a *specific* valid order (rather than just *a* valid order) is making an assumption the problem likely never promised.

Second, and more dangerous: running a topological sort without checking for a cycle first (or checking the output length after). On a graph with a cycle, Kahn's algorithm will simply terminate early with a partial, incomplete order and no error — and DFS-based sort, without an explicit gray/black check layered on top, can silently produce a garbage order rather than any indication something's wrong. Always verify the input is actually a DAG (or check the output covers all n nodes) before trusting the result.
